questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Identify what recognition requires of an audience's knowledge.
questions.stem: In a revision group, one student says a plot is well made when the audience understands it completely. What do the others say recognition requires?

options.text: That the ending must be completely unpredictable for the audience
options.misconception: confuses an information gap with total surprise

options.text: That every character must understand the plot before the end
options.misconception: shifts the requirement from the audience to the characters

options.text: That some knowledge must be held back until the moment of recognition
That the plot should be explained fully at the beginning
options.misconception: prefers exposition to a withheld reveal

questions.explanation: Recognition needs a gap: the audience must know less than the resolution will reveal. Total unpredictability, characters' understanding and early explanation each describe something else.
questions.hint: Ask what the audience must lack before the reveal.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Deus ex machina and the objection to it
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a resolution imported from outside is objected to.
questions.stem: A revision group discusses a play in which a stranger arrives at the end with a letter that explains everything. Why do they call the solution deus ex machina?

answer.exemplar: The group calls it deus ex machina because the resolution arrives from outside the action rather than from anything the story has built. The stranger has no history with the characters, his letter carries the explanation wholesale, and the machinery is therefore lowered onto the plot at the moment it is needed, which is the classic objection to a rescue by convenience.

questions.explanation: The device is named when the resolution is imported from outside rather than prepared by the action, and a stranger's letter is the clearest case. The group is diagnosing a structural shortcut.
questions.hint: Ask where the explanation came from.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate an explanation of a fall in terms of textual support.
questions.stem: A revision group hears a student explain a heroine's disaster by her pride. Which reply do the others consider stronger?

options.text: The reply holds because pride is the classic flaw in such stories
options.misconception: leans on convention rather than on the text's evidence

options.text: The reply holds if the text supports it, since a flaw must be shown to cause the fall
The reply holds because the heroine boasts openly before the catastrophe
options.misconception: treats one boast as the whole explanation

options.text: The reply holds because pride explains the plot in a single phrase
options.misconception: prefers a tidy explanation to a tested one

questions.explanation: A tragic flaw is an explanation the text must support, so pride counts only if the play shows it driving the catastrophe. Convention, a single boast and convenience each fail that test.
questions.hint: Ask what the text shows about the flaw.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a structural cause from a personal defect.

stimulus.body: The group is reading a scene in which a clerk is ruined by rules he wrote himself, and the rules turn out to have been written by a board that was abolished years earlier and whose abolition was hidden from everyone on the floor. options.text: the clerk's lack of imagination, which kept him from questioning the rules
options.misconception: rephrases a structural cause as a personal defect

options.text: the clerk's loyalty to his seniors, which stopped him asking who ruled
options.misconception: attributes an institutional failure to a personal virtue

questions.explanation: The rule survived because its abolition was hidden, so the cause sits in the institution rather than in the clerk's character. Personal virtues describe the man, not the mechanism.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Analyse the argumentative work a pun performs.
questions.stem: During the discussion, a name spoken twice in a scene, once for a war and once for a lover. Why does the group find the pun worth analysing?

answer.exemplar: The group finds it worth analysing because a pun sets two meanings side by side in a single stretch of speech, so the audience hears both at once. The double sense links the war and the lover in the character's mouth, and that linking is argument rather than decoration, because it makes a private attachment and a public cause occupy the same word in the scene.

questions.explanation: A pun makes two meanings available at the same moment, so it can carry an argument a plain statement would only state. The group is analysing a tool, not a joke.
questions.hint: Ask what two meanings the word holds at once.

questions.explanation: A mystery plays on the distance between the audience's guess and the proof, so an early suspicion is part of the experience. Defeating guesses and withholding clues are other claims.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a foil reveals by contrast.
questions.stem: The group compares a foolish knight in a serious play with a serious official in a comedy. What do they conclude the pair demonstrates?

answer.exemplar: The pair demonstrates that a foil reveals by contrast rather than by argument. The knight's seriousness in a serious play and the official's folly in a comedy each make the surrounding qualities more legible, because the audience measures one character against the nearest one, and the play gains a second reading of its own tone while it does so.

questions.explanation: A foil works by placing a contrasting trait close enough to measure the original, and both cases show that rather than an argument about the trait. Tone and contrast are what the pair shows.
questions.hint: Ask what each character measures the other by.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a pun's two meanings do to one another.
questions.stem: The group discusses a scene in which a woman says she will not go back to the house, and the phrase means both a building and a family. What do they conclude the phrase does?

answer.exemplar: The group concludes that the two meanings work together and comment on each other, which is why the phrase carries an argument as well as a pleasure. questions.explanation: When two meanings work together, each comments on the other, so the pun carries argument as well as wordplay. Confusion, verbal cleverness and a planted hint each narrow what the device does.

questions.explanation: A foil reveals by contrast, so the doctor's cynicism makes the patient's hope measurable rather than merely stated. Realism and self-deception are claims the pairing does not make.

options.text: The reply fails, because the distance between suspicion and proof is the tension
The reply fails, because readers enjoy being surprised more than being right
options.misconception: settles the question with audience preference

questions.explanation: A mystery plays on the distance between suspicion and proof, so an early suspicion is part of the experience rather than a spoiler. Wrong guesses and readerly taste are other claims.
questions.hint: Ask what happens between suspicion and proof.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Deus ex machina and the objection to it
questions.learningObjective: Identify why a resolution imported from outside is objected to.

stimulus.body: The group reads a play in which the heroine is about to be convicted when a stranger's letter arrives stating that the witness who condemned her has been dead for a year. The group notes that the letter is delivered, read and acted upon within a single scene, and that the stranger is never seen again.

questions.stem: On the group's reading, one letter's function is

options.text: to reveal a fact the audience has been waiting for since act one
options.misconception: credits a truth reveal without asking its authority

options.text: to supply the resolution from outside anything the play has prepared
to give the hero a chance to show her innocence at the last moment
options.misconception: reduces the device to the effect on one character

options.text: to demonstrate that the court's procedure could be defeated by a letter
options.misconception: reads a literary device as a claim about institutions

questions.explanation: The letter arrives from outside the play's action, with no prior history and no cost, and it settles the case at once, which is the classic imported resolution. Truth and procedure are other readings.
questions.hint: Ask what prepared the letter.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Choose between explanations by the evidence the play supplies.
questions.stem: The group weighs two explanations of a captain's loss: his temper, which the play shows three times, and a chart error, which the play shows once and then corrects.

options.text: That the temper explains the loss, since the play shows it three times
options.misconception: counts occurrences instead of weighing what the text shows

options.text: That the chart error explains the loss, because a chart can sink any vessel
options.misconception: credits an impersonal cause with greater force on principle

options.text: That the two explanations are equal, since the captain dies in both of them
options.misconception: treats a shared outcome as shared evidence

options.text: That the better explanation is the one the play supports with evidence

questions.explanation: An explanation must be judged by what the play supports, so the group weighs evidence rather than counting appearances or generalising about charts. A shared outcome is not shared evidence.
questions.hint: Ask which account the play supports.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate how character and structure should be weighed.
questions.stem: One student explains a family's collapse collapse by the elder son's greed, and another by a trade that collapsed two years earlier.

options.text: The group should ask what the play shows about choices within the conditions
The greedy account is better, since character explains action more deeply
options.misconception: prefers psychological depth over textual evidence

options.text: The trade account is better, since economics decides every collapse
options.misconception: generalises a structural cause into a universal rule

options.text: Both are equally good, since the group has not read the last chapter
options.misconception: treats unread evidence as no evidence at all

questions.explanation: An explanation must be judged by what the play supports, and the play can show personal choices made inside inherited conditions. Depth and unread evidence avoid that test.
questions.hint: Ask what the play shows about choices inside the conditions.
